Top (Red): mass spectra of ethylene glycol standard; Bottom (Green), mass spectra of the product of in vitro reaction at a retention time corresponding to that of ethylene glycol standard. 45 This represents a key milestone in which USF has shown ethylene glycol production from formate in vitro (10 ML.1), demonstrating the feasibility of the designed pathway to support the overall required biological conversion. To further probe the overall pathway and identify potential bottlenecks, the concentration of co-factors and enzymes was then varied to determine the impact on overall ethylene glycol production. As seen in Figure 31, while increasing the amount of LmACR and FucO contained in the reaction mixture had minimal impact, increasing the NADH concentration (1.5 and 2-fold) resulted in a corresponding increase in ethylene glycol production. Given the requirement for reducing equivalents resulting from the higher degree of reduction per carbon of ethylene glycol compared to formate, this result was expected and demonstrates how additional electrons can maximize the overall conversion. This is also apparent in reactions in which the CoA donor required for formyl-CoA generation from formate was increased. While no increase in ethylene glycol was observed upon increasing the CoA donor alone, increasing both the CoA and NADH resulted in the highest ethylene glycol titer (Figure 31). Based on these results, efficiently generating both formyl-CoA and ensuring sufficient NADH supply are key considerations for pathway operation. We are currently evaluating additional enzymes for formyl-CoA generation as well as NADH-dependent formate dehydrogenases that can be exploited to generate the required NADH. Engineer microorganisms for formate to ethylene glycol conversion (Task 11) Our ethylene glycol (EG) production pathway consists of three modules: C1 activation, condensation to glycolyl-CoA (C2), and product synthesis.
